title: Hamas Agreed to Disarm. Why Did Israel Reject the Deal?
gist: Hamas accepted a US-backed disarmament framework that Trump called 'HISTORIC,' but Netanyahu rejected it within days, and experts say Israel's position cannot shift before October elections — and probably not much after. Israel controls more than 60 percent of Gaza with orders to reach 70 percent, the Board of Peace has already conceded that IDF withdrawal waits until decommissioning is complete, and the verification bodies (NCAG, ISF) either sit stranded in Cairo or do not yet exist.

themes.theme: Israeli electoral calendar as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Israel's position on the Hamas disarmament framework is extremely unlikely to change before the country's October elections, because Netanyahu's coalition promised voters absolute victory and cannot be seen conceding to Hamas.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: October 2026 is the earliest realistic date for any Gaza policy inflection — treat all interim peace headlines as noise for positioning in Israeli assets and regional risk.
insights.quote: The problem is that politically, in Israel, and especially before elections, it’s borderline impossible for the Israeli government to accept [the plan],
insights.locator: Experts told Foreign Policy that Israel’s position

insights.claim: Even a post-election government replacing Netanyahu would be hard-pressed to make major Gaza concessions, so a change of Israeli leadership is not a sufficient catalyst for the peace process.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Do not price an Israeli election result as a peace catalyst; the constraint is public opinion, not one prime minister.
insights.quote: A new government would be hard-pressed to suddenly make major concessions in Gaza,
insights.locator: But even if Netanyahu loses in October

insights.claim: Netanyahu explicitly stated Israel will not withdraw from its current lines until Hamas is completely disarmed, inverting the framework's sequencing of phased withdrawal alongside decommissioning.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Sequencing is the whole deal: 'disarm first, withdraw later' is a demand Hamas has never accepted, so the framework is structurally stalled.
insights.locator: In the days since, Israel has expressed strong opposition

insights.claim: Trump publicly claimed Israel was 'very happy' with the agreement one day after announcing it, a claim contradicted within days by Israeli statements and airstrikes in Gaza.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Discount US presidential characterizations of counterparty consent in this process; verify against the counterparty's own statements before repricing risk.
insights.quote: The next day, Trump said that Israel was “very happy” with the agreement.
insights.locator: For a moment last week, it looked like change

themes.theme: Facts on the ground favor continued occupation

insights.claim: Israel controls more than 60 percent of Gaza and Netanyahu directed the IDF in May to expand control to 70 percent, with the supposedly temporary yellow line pushed further into the territory in recent weeks.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Territorial expansion orders are the clearest revealed preference: Israel is planning an extended stay, not a withdrawal — the reconstruction trade stays off the table.
insights.quote: Israel is currently estimated to control more than 60 percent of the coastal enclave.
insights.locator: But there are many reasons to believe that Israel

insights.claim: The Board of Peace has already conceded Israel's core demand, posting that IDF withdrawal beyond the yellow line occurs only once decommissioning is complete — reversing its initial push for simultaneous steps.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: The mediator folding within days shows where leverage actually sits; expect further US concessions to Israel rather than pressure on it.
insights.quote: The withdrawal of the IDF beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators,
insights.locator: As Netanyahu outright rejects the plan

insights.claim: A ceasefire that began in October 2025 has left Gaza in painful limbo for roughly ten months because Hamas disarmament, the precondition for major parts of Trump's 20-point plan, was never resolved.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Ten months of stalemate establishes the base rate: assume continued limbo absent a structural change in one side's incentives.
insights.locator: For months, Hamas’s disarmament has been the biggest sticking point

themes.theme: Verification architecture that does not exist

insights.claim: The disarmament plan requires Hamas's weapons to be stored inside Gaza under supervision of the NCAG, a body Israel has blocked from entering Gaza whose 15 members remain stuck in Cairo.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
entities: National Committee for the Administration of Gaza
insights.so_what: The designated administrator cannot physically reach the territory it is meant to administer — a hard, checkable gating item for whether the plan is real.
insights.locator: The disarmament agreement calls for the process

insights.claim: Israel regards storing Hamas arms in Gaza under NCAG supervision as 'a joke' because it removes Israel from monitoring while concerns persist that Hamas is rearming and rebuilding.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Any workable framework must give Israel a monitoring role; proposals that exclude it are dead on arrival regardless of Hamas's agreement.
insights.locator: Efron said that from Israel’s perspective

insights.claim: The framework only begins after deployment of an international stabilization force that does not yet exist, despite Israel reportedly giving initial approval in late July for some form of multinational force.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: The plan's trigger condition is unmet and unscheduled — ISF force generation is the concrete milestone to watch before believing any timeline.
insights.locator: The framework also states that the process will begin

insights.claim: Qatar and Turkey's potential role in the verification mechanism is itself disqualifying for Israel, where Qatar is viewed as a borderline enemy state and some see Turkey as the 'new Iran.'
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: The only actors with leverage over Hamas are the ones Israel will not accept as verifiers — a structural deadlock, not a negotiating gap.
insights.quote: In the Israeli minds of today, Qatar is a borderline enemy state and Turkey the same,
insights.locator: The deal is also unpalatable to Israel

insights.claim: Hamas's agreement to disarm was surprising because arms are central to its identity as a resistance movement, suggesting the move was tactical rather than a genuine capitulation.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Read the concession as blame-shifting positioning; do not extrapolate to Hamas actually decommissioning weapons.
insights.quote: The group defines itself as a resistance movement, and arms are central to its identity.
insights.locator: That’s in part because few expected Hamas to agree

insights.claim: Hamas likely never expected Netanyahu to accept the framework and used it to put the onus on Israel and shift blame for the lack of progress in Gaza.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: A cheap, effective information operation: expect more such 'acceptances' from Hamas designed to isolate Israel diplomatically at low real cost.
insights.locator: Some speculate that Hamas never expected Netanyahu

insights.claim: Even a calculated Hamas move changed the dynamic in a necessary way and gives the Board of Peace and the United States new leverage over Israel if they choose to use it, such as trading NCAG entry for heavy-weapons decommissioning.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: The optimistic case rests entirely on US willingness to pressure Israel — a conditional that has repeatedly failed in this process.
insights.quote: We can be clear-eyed about the fact that this is not going to suddenly resolve things in Gaza. Hamas is not going to bury or turn over their arms tomorrow. Israel is not going to be withdrawing anytime soon,
insights.locator: Yet some experts said that the disarmament plan

insights.claim: Trump's framework follows a recurring pattern of an initial announcement built on a one-pager of bullet points with details to be hashed out later, an approach that has already failed in Gaza and Iran.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for pricing Trump-branded diplomatic breakthroughs: no implementation detail means no tradeable change until verification bodies physically deploy.
insights.quote: You see this initial announcement, a one-pager of bullet points, and then this idea that the rest of it will be hashed out later,

insights.claim: Trump's enthusiastic announcement of the framework was a hardball tactic to bully a way forward, representing noise rather than actual movement in the conflict.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Fade the headline: announced agreements without counterparty consent are negotiating pressure, not state changes.
insights.quote: This development represents “noise” but “no movement,” Brown said.
insights.locator: Nathan J. Brown, a professor of political science

insights.claim: The Board of Peace's own Gaza representative concedes this is the start of the hard phase and that the work ahead is grinding and technical, tempering expectations of near-term resolution.
insights.speaker: John Haltiwanger
insights.so_what: Even the mediator is guiding expectations down — a signal to extend any assumed timeline for Gaza reconstruction or regional normalization trades.
